title: TC0-04044
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): She appeals a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) rejecting her claim for refugee protection.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: The Appellant, XXXX XXXX XXXX, a.k.a. XXXX XXXX XXXX, claims to be a citizen of Ethiopia. She appeals a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) rejecting her claim for refugee protection. The Appellant has not submitted new evidence pursuant to subsection 110(4) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA), nor has she requested an oral hearing under subsection 110(6) before the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD). The Appellant asks the RAD to substitute a finding that she is a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection. In the alternative, the Appellant asks the RAD to refer the matter back to the RPD for redetermination.
I dismiss the appeal. The RPD was correct in finding that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection. The determinative issues are identity and credibility.

The Appellant claims she fears persecution in Ethiopia due to her anti-government opinion as well as her Oromo ethnicity. Beginning in October 2014, the Appellant claims she worked as a XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX. Following protests on October 3, 2016 where protestors were fired upon, the Appellant treated the injured in her role as a XXXX. She states that she was detained on October 4, 2016, during which time she was interrogated and accused of passing information to opposition parties. She states that she was held for 11 days, after which time she was dismissed from her job on order of the local administration. On September 22, 2017, the Appellant's father, an anti-government activist, disappeared. On October 1, 2017, the family was told by police to collect his body and not have the cause of his death examined. On October 5, 2017, the police went to the Appellant's home and brought her and her mother into detention, where they were held for one week. With the assistance of an agent, the Appellant left Ethiopia on what she claims is a false passport with a Canadian temporary resident visa in the alternate name of XXXX XXXX XXXX with an alternate date of birth of XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX. She arrived in Canada on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2017 and made the present claim for refugee protection in the name of XXXX XXXX XXXX on December 14, 2017.1

On June 26, 2019, the Minister of Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) filed an intervention with respect to the Appellant's claim, and provided evidence that she had previously used two Ethiopian passports in an alternate identity (alternate names and dates of birth) for visa applications to the United States (U.S.) and Canada, as confirmed by Canadian records and a biometric fingerprint match with U.S. records.2

By way of a written decision dated January 24, 2020, the RPD rejected the Appellant's claim on the basis of identity and credibility, finding that the Appellant had not discharged her burden to prove her identity on a balance of probabilities.3 It is from that negative decision that the Appellant now appeals. ANALYSIS Role of the RAD
My role is to look at all the evidence and decide if the RPD made the correct decision.4

For the reasons set out below, I agree with the RPD and find that the RPD was correct in determining that the Appellant had not established her personal or national identity on a balance of probabilities. Merits of the Appeal The Appellant's alternate Ethiopian passports - the Minister's evidence
The Appellant presently claims her personal identity to be XXXX XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX.5

The Minister's evidence6 shows that the Appellant used Ethiopian passport #XXXX in the name of XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, to apply for and obtain a Canadian temporary resident visa, and to enter Canada on XXXX XXXX, 2017. This passport was submitted for document analysis and has been verified as genuine, although it could not be determined if the passport was nonetheless improperly issued by a competent authority, or improperly obtained through fraud.7 However, the genuineness of the passport itself (as a whole including the photo) contradicts the Appellant's testimony about the passport, which was that she obtained this passport with the assistance of an agent and that all the passport information was fraudulent but for the photo of herself, which is genuine.8 At her hearing, the Appellant testified she knows nothing of the details about this passport or visa, or how it was obtained by the agent.

The Minister's evidence also shows that the Appellant used Ethiopian passport XXXX XXXX in the name of XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, to apply for visas to the United States (U.S.), which were twice rejected.9 This information was obtained through a biometric fingerprint comparison which yielded an exact match to the Appellant's refugee fingerprints taken in Canada.10 This information conflicts with the Appellant's sworn refugee intake statements, where she indicated she had never been refused a visa by any country.11 U.S. records also indicate that the Appellant represented in her U.S. visa application that she is married, and provided the name of her spouse, the names of her father as XXXX XXXX and her mother as XXXX XXXX, her city of residence, and stated her occupation in XXXX,12 nearly all of which are inconsistent with the personal details declared by the Appellant in her refugee claim, made under a very similar name, although slightly different spelling, but with an alternate date of birth. A review of the audio recording of the Appellant's RPD hearing indicates that the Appellant testified that she applied for the passport that she used to apply for her U.S. visa with the agent, and that she was aware that there were "errors" on it, but that she did not make efforts to correct them.

In the present appeal, the Appellant alleges that the RPD erred in paragraph 17 of its decision by "holding against [her]" that she made Canadian immigration authorities aware that she was travelling on a false passport on arrival.13 She makes no further argument on this point. On my review of the RPD decision at paragraph 17, indeed of the decision as a whole, I see no such error. The RPD was providing in that paragraph one example of how the Appellant's answers regarding the details of her arrival in Canada were inconsistent with the facts on record and therefore not credible; as the RPD stated, her explanations were "neither straightforward nor trustworthy."14 As such, the RPD did not fault the Appellant simply for making immigration authorities aware that she had entered Canada on a false passport; rather, it was the cumulation of evidence about two alternate passports, inconsistencies between that evidence and the Appellant's evidence, and the lack of a reasonable explanation provided by the Appellant, on which the RPD based its negative finding on identity. I cannot find that the RPD erred as alleged.

The Appellant also alleges that the RPD erred in faulting the Appellant for being unable to state the duration of time for which she was admitted to Canada, when the duration was not stamped on her passport.15 To provide context to the RPD's findings in paragraph 22, the RPD had questioned the Appellant regarding how long she was admitted into Canada for upon her arrival, a question which she could not answer, and instead indicated repeatedly that she thought she could stay forever. Evidence provided by the Minister indicates that the Appellant's admission to Canada was restricted to a period considerably shorter than what her visa would normally allow, indicating concern as to the Appellant's motives for entering Canada on the part of the immigration officer who admitted her.16 The RPD's conclusion was that the Appellant's response to the Panel's questions about how long she was admitted to Canada for was "vague and evasive".17 A review of the hearing indicates that the Appellant simply responded several times to the effect that upon arrival in Canada she thought she could stay forever.

While I find no error on the part of the RPD in its conclusion that the Appellant's testimony was vague and evasive, indeed I find this conclusion to be correct, I also find that this point is not determinative. The length of time for which the Appellant was admitted into Canada, whether she was aware that her admittance was restricted to a period considerably shorter than what her visa would typically allow or not, is not central to the issue of her identity nor is it determinative of her credibility. In the RAD's view, the factual basis for the RPD's negative decision on identity - which is US and Canadian immigration records which both reflect different names, dates of birth, and personal details for the Appellant than those with which she has made her present refugee claim - were issues which were not adequately or reasonably explained by the Appellant. Whether or not the Appellant had actual knowledge that her admission to Canada was restricted upon entry, is a peripheral credibility issue. As will continue to be set out below, the Appellant has failed to discharge her burden to prove her identity with credible and trustworthy evidence, on a balance of probabilities.

With respect to the Appellant's identity as set out in the passport evidence provided by the Minister, the Appellant submits that the RPD erred in finding either of the passports to be determinative of her identity,18 and that the RPD erred in finding that the "passport she used to come to Canada was probably genuine."19 However, a plain reading of the RPD's decision shows this is not the case: while the RPD indicates that the evidence before the Panel was not satisfactorily explained and therefore raised the "very real possibility" that the Appellant's true name is XXXX XXXX XXXX, as reflected on her verified genuine Ethiopian passport used to travel to Canada,20 the RPD ultimately made the explicit finding that the determinative issue is that Appellant did not discharge her burden to prove her identity on a balance of probabilities.21 The RPD did not make a determination as to which (if any) of the competing identities were the Appellant's true identity, a finding which is not required in any case as the burden remains with the Appellant. As such, the RPD did not err as alleged.

The Appellant also alleges that the RPD erred in failing to apply the Gender Guidelines and consider that the Appellant's testimony would be impacted by her psychological state given the letter from a nurse at XXXX XXXX XXXX who has treated the Appellant.22 The Appellant does not provide further argument on this point. A review of the letter indicates simply that the Appellant has been seen at the hospital's clinic for newly arrived refugees since February 2018 to address "XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX and that "Ms. XXXX is particularly concerned about her XXXX XXXX in the context of her basis of claim and how that affects her current daily function." 23 The letter contains no diagnosis, nor does it indicate any medical opinion on how the Appellant's mental health might affect her hearing or her ability to give evidence, other than to indicate that the Appellant herself - as opposed to the nurse treating her - has a concern about XXXX XXXX in the context of her basis of claim. After a review of the Appellant's hearing and the full RPD record, I am not persuaded that the RPD erred in failing to consider how this evidence might affect the Appellant's ability to give coherent testimony, as the letter does not indicate that that is a medical concern diagnosed by the treating professional, only that it is a concern of the Appellant. I am likewise not persuaded that the RPD erred in applying the Gender Guidelines by failing to explicitly consider this evidence, given the vague and unspecific content of the letter.

The RPD's finding that the Appellant has not proven her identity on a balance of probabilities relates centrally to the evidence provided by the Minister in the form of Canadian and US immigration records for the Appellant which are inconsistent as between them, and are also inconsistent with the identity details and personal details provided by the Appellant in her present refugee claim, which were not reasonably explained by the Appellant. She did not indicate that she has any medical or mental health diagnosis which would affect her ability to give testimony at her hearing, nor did she indicate before or during the hearing that was having memory issues, or that she forgot to include or disclose information, nor do I find support for the fact that these concerns would be properly attributable to either insomnia or poor concentration. As such, after considering the Appellant's mental health evidence, I do not find that the RPD erred as alleged.

It is worth noting here that the Appellant has raised the same argument in regard to the Gender Guidelines and consideration of the letter from XXXX XXXX XXXX in the context of the RPD's conclusions on her Kebele ID card24 and her birth certificate,25 and for the same reasons I find no such error by the RPD. The letter from XXXX XXXX XXXX provides insufficient evidence to suggest that the Appellant has any mental health diagnoses which would or could affect her ability to provide clear and consistent evidence, and I cannot find that the RPD erred by not explicitly considering the letter in the context of the Appellant's ability to give evidence. Kebele ID card and birth certificate

The Appellant submitted a birth certificate in the name of XXXX (no surname noted), date of birth XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX,26 which the Minister submits converts to XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX in the Gregorian calendar.27 However, the birth certificate reflects that it was issued December 21, 2017, nearly 25 years after the Appellant's birth and a month after the Appellant arrived in Canada. When the Panel asked the Appellant why it was issued so long after her birth, she replied that she did not ask for it herself, but that her mother obtained it for her. The RPD found the Appellant was vague and evasive in her response.28 The Appellant does not challenge the RPD's finding in respect of her birth certificate, except to allege that the RPD erred in impugning her explanation by failing to apply the Gender Guidelines by not considering how her evidence would be affected by her mental health, as set out above. I do not find that the Appellant's memory problems, insomnia, or poor concentration would impact this answer, nor does the Appellant state how her mental health may have affected her evidence, and I find the RPD was correct in concluding that the Appellant did not reasonably explain the late issuance of her birth certificate. As such, I also find the birth certificate is of diminished evidentiary value due to its significantly late issuance not contemporaneous with the Appellant's birth which was not reasonably explained by her, as well as for the fact that it does not speak to her full name. I find this item does not overcome the credibility concerns arising from the Minister's evidence with respect to the Appellant's identity, such that it does not prove her identity on a balance of probabilities, even when considered cumulatively with the other documents submitted by the Appellant, as discussed below.

The Appellant also provided a Kebele identity card in the name of XXXX XXXX XXXX, listing her year of birth as 1992, with no specific date.29 The RPD found that the translated Kebele identity card lacked credibility given that the original card itself spells her name in the Roman alphabet as "XXXX XXXX XXXX", and the translation indicates it as "XXXX XXXX XXXX". The Appellant alleges that in so finding, the RPD erred as the writing on the card is in Oromo, and although it uses the Roman alphabet, the Appellant's name would still be spelled differently in English.30 However, the RAD notes that the Appellant had also indicated on her refugee intake form that in her native language, the spelling of her name would be "XXXX XXXX XXXX."31 At her RPD hearing, the Appellant testified that the spelling of her name on her Kebele identity card is not right because there is "o" at the end of her surname on the card. The Appellant's statements at her hearing and on her refugee intake form with respect to the spelling of her name on her Kebele card therefore do not support her present argument that "XXXX XXXX XXXX" in Oromo translates to "XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX in English. In light of the Appellant's own prior statements, including specifically her admission at her hearing that her Kebele card misspells her name, I cannot agree with her present argument that the RPD erred as alleged. I find the RPD was correct in assigning little weight to her Kebele card in support of her identity.

Moreover, the RPD had concerns with the date of issuance of the Appellant's Kebele card, given that it purports to have been issued on December 11, 2017, one month after the Appellant had arrived in Canada. The RPD drew a negative credibility inference against the Appellant for not explaining why she did not have a previous Kebele identity card to submit, given the importance of these cards to everyday life in Ethiopia.32 The Appellant argues the RPD erred in discounting the Kebele card on the basis that it was issued after the Appellant's arrival in Canada, as that "does not mean the card is false."33 The Appellant also asserts that the RPD erred by ignoring her previous Kebele card which was filed in evidence, citing Exhibit C-9, p.1-3.34 The translated copy of the earlier Kebele identity card35 appears to have been issued "11/12/2013" and states the Appellant's name as XXXX XXXX XXXX, and her mother's name as XXXX. While I would set aside the RPD's negative inference from the erroneous observation that the Appellant had not submitted an earlier Kebele card, I cannot ascribe full evidentiary value to it, as some information appears to be missing from that card, such as her age, ethnic background, and the phone number for her emergency contact. In addition, both the photo on the front and the entire back of the card are illegible (as written on the copies submitted).36

I am not prepared to find that the Appellant's partially-illegible earlier Kebele identity card, even coupled with her subsequent Kebele identity card issued after her arrival in Canada, constitute credible and trustworthy evidence which is sufficient to overcome the credibility concerns arising from the Appellant's unreasonably explained past use of Ethiopian passports in alternate identities. This is especially so where one of the past passports her fingerprints are associated with bears a name remarkably similar to the name which she currently claims is her true name, but with an alternate date of birth and alternate personal details, and another passport which has been verified as genuine but bears entirely identity information with the Appellant's genuine photo. I am not prepared to find that the Kebele cards and/or birth certificate submitted by the Appellant are sufficiently trustworthy and credible to allow me to find that they establish her identity on a balance of probabilities. Other supporting documents do not benefit from the presumption of genuineness, given the totality of the evidence

The Appellant argues that the RPD erred by failing to explicitly consider her other identity documents submitted, beyond its analysis and rejection of her Kebele identity card and birth certificate. Although the RPD indicated in its reasons that the Panel had found the Appellant had not proven her identity on a balance of probabilities after having undertaken a "close examination" of the "documents filed in Exhibits C-4, C-9, C-10, and C-11,"37 (her supporting identity documents) she argues that the RPD erred in not analyzing each of her supporting items explicitly, including specifically her driver's license, student transcripts, and nursing license, which she argues are "official" and therefore benefit from the presumption of genuineness as items which are issued by a foreign government.38 She claims in this appeal that the RPD identified no issues with these documents, and therefore, having failed to make findings specifically relating to these documents, they constitute sufficient persuasive evidence of her personal and national identity.39

The Federal Court has held that where the RPD is satisfied that one or more of an applicant's identity documents have been fraudulently obtained or are otherwise inauthentic, the presumption that the applicant's remaining identity documents are valid can no longer be maintained. Notwithstanding, the RPD and the RAD are still required to at least consider and assess the authenticity and probative value of each of those documents, as well as any other supporting documents submitted by the Appellant. 40

I agree with the findings of the RPD above. Micheal CraneGiven the evidence on record indicates that the Appellant has used Ethiopian passports in two alternate names with two alternate dates of birth, which do not match the identity the Appellant is currently claiming to be her true identity, and given that she has provided no reasonable explanation therefor, I cannot find that her remaining secondary documents are - individually or cumulatively - sufficient to establish her identity on a balance of probabilities. However, in my own assessment of the evidence, I have examined each of the Appellant's documents, and set out my findings below.

The Appellant invited the RAD to consider her driver's license, and suggested that being issued by a foreign government, it benefits from the presumption of truthfulness with respect to establishing her identity. However, it is apparent on the face of the document that the driver's license purports to have been issued to the Appellant on October 12, 2016,41 which is inconsistent with the Appellant's Basis of Claim (BOC) Narrative, where she states that she was detained and mistreated by Ethiopian authorities from October 4 to 14, 2016.42 Therefore, in addition to the significant and persisting credibility concerns noted above, I find there are prima facie credibility concerns with respect to the additional identity document the Appellant specifically relies upon, her driver's license, to establish her identity.

The Appellant also invited the RAD to specifically consider her student transcripts and her nursing license, and after a review of the entirety of the Appellant's secondary identity documents, I am not persuaded that these or any of the items overcome the credibility concerns noted so as to establish her identity on a balance of probabilities. The Appellant's educational documents43 state her name as XXXX XXXX XXXX but provide no date of birth and contain no security features, which diminishes their evidentiary value. Likewise, her employment documents44 and XXXX license45 list her name but provide no date of birth or personal/family details that would support the Appellant's current identity claim, and also contain no security features that would justify significant evidentiary value being assigned to them. The Appellant's baptismal certificate46 provides an alternate spelling of her name as XXXX XXXX XXXX and states her mother's name as XXXX XXXX and father's name as XXXX XXXX XXXX making no mention of their shared surname "XXXX" as asserted by the Appellant in her BOC.47 Given that I agree with the RPD's finding with respect to the significant problems with the Appellant's central identity documents, compounded by the low probative value and diminished reliability of the Appellant's secondary identity documents, I find that even in their totality these items cannot overcome the persisting credibility concerns with respect to the Appellant's identity and do not establish her identity on a balance of probabilities. Other issues raised on appeal

The Appellant also relies on Canadian jurisprudence which holds that the RPD errs where it draws a negative inference against a claimant simply on the basis that the claimant used false documents to travel to Canada and seek protection; the Appellant argues that the RPD erred by doing so in her case.48 However, this is not the case for the Appellant. The negative inferences made by the RPD with respect to the allegedly false documents used by the Appellant with respect to her applications for a visa to the U.S., and then for a visa and travel to Canada, were not made solely or simply on her use thereof, but rather also include consideration of her lack of reasonable explanation for inconsistencies in the evidence, and concerns with the documents submitted by the Appellant herself.

The RPD articulated credibility concerns about where the Appellant's evidence is inconsistent with the Minister's evidence; for instance, her assertion in her Canadian refugee intake forms that she had never been refused a visa to any country49 when the Minister's evidence shows she was twice refused a visa to the US in an identity bearing a name very similar to the name she uses now. While it is clear that she indicated on her Basis of Claim form that she had had a U.S. visa application rejected, her BOC makes no reference that she had made these claims in an alternate or false identity.50

In addition, the RPD had concerns about the Appellant's assertion that she had never had a genuine Ethiopian passport and that the passport she used to come to Canada was fraudulent, but for her photo which was genuine, whereas the Minister's evidence indicates that the passport was analyzed as genuine. The RPD also had concerns about aspects of the Appellant's own documents, including her birth certificate and Kebele identity card, both of which were issued in Ethiopia after her arrival in Canada, and for which the Appellant provided no reasonable explanation other than to indicate that her mother obtained them for her.

To this I would also add the RAD's credibility concern apparent on the face of the Appellant's driver's license, which indicates that it was issued to her in Ethiopia during the period which she states she was jailed. I would also note after my own review of the evidence that while much of the Appellant's personal and family details are different between her three identities used for different immigration processes,51 there is some concerning overlap. For instance, her Canadian visa application in the identity of XXXX XXXX XXXX lists her as a married woman, with her spouse's surname as "XXXX,"52 demonstrating some degree of cross-reference as between the alternate identities the Appellant has used. Therefore, in consideration of the totality of the evidence, I cannot agree with the Appellant that the RPD erred in faulting her simply for using false or fraudulent documents to seek protection abroad.

Lastly, the Appellant argues that the RPD identified no issues with respect to her credibility based on her allegations and stated that "[t]here were no contradictions."53 For the same reasons set out above, I cannot agree. The RPD had numerous issues with the Appellant's credibility, and for which the Appellant was unable to give reasonable explanations when they were put to her at the hearing. These credibility concerns I have found were clearly grounded in the evidence on record and relate to the foundational allegation of who the Appellant is.

The RPD found that there was insufficient persuasive evidence to establish the Appellant's identity, on a balance of probabilities. On the basis of the findings noted above and after my own assessment of all the evidence, including the Appellant's oral evidence at the RPD hearings and the documentary evidence submitted by the Appellant and the Minister, I agree with the finding of the RPD that the Appellant has not established her identity with credible and trustworthy evidence, on a balance of probabilities.

As identity is a threshold issue, I therefore find that the Appellant has failed to establish a well-founded fear of persecution under section 96 of the IRPA, and for the same reasons, I find that the Appellant is not a person in need of protection under section 97 of the IRPA.

I dismiss the appeal and confirm the decision of the RPD that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection, pursuant to section 111(1)(a) of the IRPA. (signed) L.
